# Fluid Frameworks (LYT)

According to Nick Milo, fluid frameworks are non-rigid, highly flexible organizing structures you apply when needed. In LYT they are mainly Higher-Order Notes such as Maps of Content and the Home Note, though a balanced mix of MOCs, folders, tags and queries can also stay fluid.

## Fluid versus rigid
- A fluid framework is a non-essential supporting structure: remove the MOC and the notes remain.
- A rigid framework such as a folder is essential: delete it and you delete its contents, and you add friction to every access.
- Fluid frameworks are not mutually exclusive. A note listed in a MOC does not live only there; it can be discovered wherever it is referenced.
- Even so, folders can be reintroduced sensibly once higher-order notes carry the linking load.

## In defence of categories
Milo answers the claim that categories are bad:
- *Categories are top-down.* A fluid category is not; notes need not fit it, and a Home note is a structure you attach to only when you care.
- *Categories are static.* MOCs arise organically when needed.
- *I have no categories.* With more than about 300 notes you do: tags, starred notes and dated daily notes are all categories. Only a vault of bare direct links has none, and Milo says the price is steep.

## Fluid taxonomies
Milo borrows the idea from Steen Comer: taxonomies can be applied on and off in a loose system and are tools, not truths. A MOC is like a temporary hierarchy that members rearrange when it stops serving.

## Daily practice
Milo says you rarely think about frameworks while writing: just make notes, maybe add a tag or a link. Build a map when the squeeze appears (see Mental Squeeze Point (LYT)).
